title: Exclusive Standing: The Bhopal Act, the Forum Moved to India, and the Settlement That Closed Every Claim
participants: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Union Carbide Corporation holds 50.9 percent of Union Carbide India Limited, with 22 percent owned or controlled by the government of India and the rest spread across some 23,500 Indian shareholders. The parent takes the return on a majority holding in a company that is, in the Second Circuit's words, "managed and operated entirely by Indians in India" — ownership in New York, operation in Madhya Pradesh.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The Bhopal plant opens in 1969 converting imported pesticides, and from 1979 or 1980 manufactures them on site, producing hazardous waste held in tanks, pits and three solar evaporation ponds on leased land. UCIL's own documents record the consequences early: in March 1982 the company is aware of leakage from one pond with another showing signs of it, and in April 1982 a UCIL document notes that "continued leakage from [an] evaporation pond [was] causing great concern".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: After the gas escapes on the night of 2-3 December 1984, the record itself is held at a distance from the claims. India's Central Bureau of Investigation seizes some 78,000 pages, of which about 36,000 are plant operation records and 1,700 pages relate to plant maintenance in 1983 and 1984. In the United States, discovery is confined to the forum question alone: Union Carbide briefs only forum non conveniens and suggests the court need not reach its other grounds, so the merits are never developed in the forum that has the parent.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Two instruments close the exposure. India's Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act of 29 March 1985 makes the Union of India the only party that may represent the victims "in India or elsewhere"; and the forum non conveniens dismissal sends every US action to the courts of that same government. The defendant now negotiates once, with a counterparty that is also a 22 percent owner of the subsidiary and a co-defendant in the Indian suits. In February 1989 the Supreme Court of India approves $470 million for "all litigations, claims, rights and liabilities related to and arising out of the [Bhopal] disaster".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The conditions that would have bound the parent are removed on appeal. The Second Circuit deletes the requirement that Union Carbide consent to enforcement of a final Indian judgment, holding it rested on an erroneous assumption and that its "minimal requirements of due process" language was ambiguous, and deletes the requirement that it submit to broad discovery under the Federal Rules while confined to narrower Indian discovery — then affirms as modified. In December 1989 the Supreme Court of India upholds the Act and the government's exclusive authority to compromise every claim; in 1993 the Second Circuit holds that the individual victims have no standing to attack the settlement made on their behalf.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Forum non conveniens as the Supreme Court had lately restated it in Gulf Oil Corp. v. Gilbert (1947) and Piper Aircraft Co. v. Reyno (1981): a plaintiff who is not a resident of the United States gets no deference for choosing a United States court, and the receiving forum need only be adequate rather than equal.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: Sovereign exclusive representation. A host state grants itself, by statute, the sole right to speak for every victim of a disaster on its soil, in its courts or anyone else's. The defendant then settles once, with a government, and that settlement is approved by that government's own highest court and held in New York to bar the people it was made for.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The parent keeps the return on a majority-owned subsidiary, answers in the forum with the lower damages, and is released by a settlement negotiated with a counterparty that is simultaneously the victims' sole representative, a 22 percent owner of the subsidiary and a defendant in the Indian actions. The objectors are told in the United States that they lack standing to question it.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the account turns on one fugitive executive — that Warren Anderson slipped out of India and that a single arrest, or extradition, would have settled it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The closure was structural, not personal. The Bhopal Act of 1985 made the Union of India the only party able to sue or compromise the civil claims, and the Supreme Court of India approved a settlement covering "all litigations, claims, rights and liabilities" arising out of the disaster. A criminal proceeding against any individual would not have reopened the civil claims that settlement discharged, which is why the Second Circuit could tell the victims in 1993 that they had no standing to challenge it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: In re Union Carbide Corp. Gas Plant Disaster at Bhopal, 809 F.2d 195 (2d Cir. 1987), affirming the forum non conveniens dismissal to India after deleting two of the district court's three conditions; the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act of 29 March 1985, granting the Union of India the exclusive right to represent the victims "in India or elsewhere"; the Supreme Court of India's orders of 14-15 February 1989 approving $470 million in settlement of all claims, and its decision of 22 December 1989 in Charan Lal Sahu upholding the Act and that exclusive authority; and Bi v. Union Carbide Chemicals & Plastics Co., 984 F.2d 582 (2d Cir. 1993), holding that the individual victims lacked standing to challenge the settlement.

citations.title: In re Union Carbide Corporation Gas Plant Disaster at Bhopal, India in December, 1984, 809 F.2d 195 (2d Cir. 1987)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full. Argued 24 November 1986, decided 14 January 1987. Opens by framing the appeal as whether claims arising from "the most devastating industrial disaster in history--the deaths of over 2,000 persons and injuries of over 200,000" should be tried in the United States or in India. States that UCIL was 50.9% owned by UCC, 22% owned or controlled by the government of India, with the balance held by about 23,500 Indian citizens, and was "managed and operated entirely by Indians in India". Records that India enacted the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act on 29 March 1985 "granting to its government, the UOI, the exclusive right to represent the victims in India or elsewhere", and that Judge Keenan dismissed on forum non conveniens on 12 May 1986 (634 F. Supp. 842) on three conditions. The court deletes two: the condition that UCC consent to enforcement of a final Indian judgment (held "predicated on an erroneous legal assumption" with ambiguous "due process" language) and the condition that UCC submit to broad discovery under the Federal Rules while confined to narrower Indian discovery. Concludes "As so modified the district court's order is affirmed." A footnote records that of 78,000 pages of documents seized by India's Central Bureau of Investigation some 36,000 are plant operation records, of which 1,700 pages relate to plant maintenance in 1983 and 1984. The opinion does not state a settlement figure — there was none yet — and does not decide any question of liability.

citations.title: Bano Bi v. Union Carbide Chemicals and Plastics Company Inc., 984 F.2d 582 (2d Cir. 1993)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full. Argued 10 November 1992, decided 26 January 1993. Frames the issue as "whether the federal and state courts of this country should defer to the judgment of a democratic foreign government that disputes arising from a mass tort occurring within its borders can be best resolved by according the foreign government exclusive standing to represent the victims of the disaster in the courts of the world", and holds: "We conclude that the plaintiffs lack standing and on that ground affirm." Records that by orders dated 14 and 15 February 1989 the Supreme Court of India approved a settlement of "all litigations, claims, rights and liabilities related to and arising out of the [Bhopal] disaster" (Union Carbide Corp. v. Union of India, 1989 [Supp.] S.C.A.L.E. 89, 90), under which "Union Carbide and UCIL agreed to pay $470 million to the Indian Government for the benefit of all victims"; that on 4 May 1989 that Court set out its reasons, being "concerned primarily that the victims of the disaster receive immediate relief"; and that on 22 December 1989, in Charan Lal Sahu v. Union of India, it "upheld the constitutional validity of the Bhopal Act and confirmed the Indian Government's exclusive authority to compromise all claims arising out of the Bhopal disaster". The appellants' grounds — that the Indian Government had a conflict of interest as part owner of UCIL, that most victims opposed the settlement as grossly inadequate, and that they had inadequate notice, inadequate representation and no opportunity to opt out — are recorded as the appellants' contentions, not as findings of the court. No per-victim distribution figure appears.

citations.title: Bano v. Union Carbide Corporation, 361 F.3d 696 (2d Cir. 2004)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full. Argued 30 October 2003, decided 17 March 2004. Confirms that the claims arising out of the gas release itself had already been dismissed as "barred by a settlement between Union Carbide and the government of India that had been approved by the Supreme Court of India", citing Bano I, 273 F.3d 120, 122 (2d Cir. 2001). The claims at issue here are the separate common-law claims for environmental injury from the plant site: the court affirms except as to Bi's claims for injury to her property, which it vacates and remands. Records that the plant opened in 1969 on two noncontiguous tracts totalling 88 acres leased from the State of Madhya Pradesh, that UCIL began manufacturing on site in 1979 or 1980, and that a UCIL document of March 1982 shows awareness of leakage from one solar evaporation pond with another showing signs of leakage, while an April 1982 UCIL document notes "continued leakage from [an] evaporation pond [was] causing great concern". It also records that a 1990 report by India's National Environmental Engineering Research Institute concluded that "no contamination of soils and ground water was observed due to the impoundment of wastewater in solar evaporation ponds" while recommending remediation — a finding against the plaintiffs on pond contamination, recorded here rather than omitted. This opinion concerns the water claims; it is not authority on the gas-release settlement beyond noting that it barred those claims.
